Coal was the largest cargo / planes landed every few minutes at its height.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: When the USSR cut all land routes to West Berlin in June 1948, American and British aircraft began flying supplies into the city through the three air corridors. They carried food, fuel and especially coal; at the height of the airlift a plane landed every few minutes. Historians estimate that about 2.3 million tonnes were flown in over some 275,000 flights before the blockade ended in May 1949.

stem: Explain why Stalin blockaded West Berlin in 1948.

points.description: Identifies Western moves to rebuild West Germany (Bizonia, Marshall Aid, Deutschmark).
Explains that Stalin feared a strong West German state, having suffered German invasion.
Identifies the aim of forcing the West out of Berlin.
Explains that West Berlin, deep in the Soviet zone, was a Western outpost and a showcase of Western prosperity.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stalin saw Bizonia, Marshall Aid and especially the new Deutschmark as steps towards a separate, strong West German state, which he feared after the German invasion of 1941. He also hoped to force the Western powers out of Berlin, which lay deep inside the Soviet zone and was a Western outpost showing off Western prosperity to East Germans.

hints: Think about the new currency and the position of Berlin.

stem: Explain the consequences of the Berlin Blockade.

points.description: Identifies a Western propaganda victory.
Explains that Stalin backed down and the USA showed it would defend allies without war.
Identifies the division of Germany into two states (1949).
Explains that the FRG and GDR made the division of Germany permanent until 1990.
Identifies NATO (1949) / the Warsaw Pact (1955).
Explains that Europe became divided between two armed alliances.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The blockade was a victory for the West: Stalin lifted it in May 1949 without gaining anything, and the USA had shown it would stand by its allies without war. It also led to the division of Germany, since in 1949 the western zones became the Federal Republic and the Soviet zone the German Democratic Republic, a split that lasted until 1990. Finally, it pushed the West to form NATO in April 1949, committing the USA to defend Western Europe; when West Germany joined in 1955 the USSR formed the Warsaw Pact, dividing Europe between two armed alliances.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source B is partly accurate. The Western powers had merged their zones, given them Marshall Aid and in June 1948 introduced the Deutschmark without Soviet agreement, and they were planning a West German state, so Stalin had real grievances. But the source is communist propaganda from the Soviet zone, written to defend Soviet policy. It calls the blockade 'measures on the roads' and hides the fact that the USSR cut off supplies to about two million people. Offering food in the Soviet sector was a way of drawing Berliners under Soviet control. Source B shows that the West provoked the crisis, but it does not prove the West was to blame, since the USSR chose to respond with a blockade of civilians.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There is a strong case against the USSR. At Yalta Stalin promised free elections in liberated Europe, but communist governments were imposed through salami tactics and rigged elections, as in Poland in 1947. The Czech coup of 1948 ended the last democracy in Eastern Europe, and the Berlin Blockade tried to force the West out of Berlin by cutting off supplies to two million civilians. This is the traditional view.

Revisionist historians point to American actions. The USA used the atomic bomb while it had a monopoly, Truman took a harder line than Roosevelt, and Marshall Aid spread American economic influence. In Germany the West merged its zones and introduced the Deutschmark without Soviet agreement, which Stalin saw as breaking Potsdam.

Post-revisionists argue that both sides acted from fear and misunderstood each other. I agree to a large extent that the USSR was more to blame, because the imposition of communist rule on Eastern Europe came first and caused most of the Western reaction; however, American policies made Soviet fears worse, so the blame was shared, though not equally.

parts.explanation: Levels: both sides, historians' views and a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), give the case against each superpower before deciding.
